title: A puzzle a child can state has stumped mathematicians since 1937
body: Take any positive whole number: if it’s even, halve it; if it’s odd, triple it and add one, and repeat. Start with 6 and you get 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Start with 27 and the sequence bounces around for 111 steps, climbing as high as 9,232, before it too sinks to 1. Lothar Collatz raised the idea in 1937, and the conjecture is that **every starting number reaches 1**. Computers have checked every start up to 2⁷¹, about 2.36 × 10²¹, but nobody has a proof, and Terence Tao showed in 2019 only that almost all starting points get almost all the way down.

slides.heading: Lothar Collatz’s rule, 1937
items: Start with any positive whole number
Odd? Triple it and add one
Repeat. The conjecture says you always reach 1

slides.question: Starting from 27, how many steps does it take to reach 1?
slides.explanation: 27 takes 111 steps and climbs as high as 9,232 on its way down to 1. Sequences like this are nicknamed hailstone numbers.

slides.heading: Steps to reach 1 from different starting numbers
slides.note: 97, 871, 6,171 and 77,031 take the most steps of any start below 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000.

slides.label: starting values checked by computer, about 2.36 × 10²¹, every one of which reaches 1
slides.text: A check is not a proof. Mathematician Jeffrey Lagarias has called the problem extraordinarily difficult and completely out of reach of present-day mathematics.
Mathematics may not be ready for such problems.

slides.clue: Nickname for Collatz sequences, which rise and fall like ice in a storm cloud before hitting the ground
slides.detail: 27 climbs as high as 9,232 before its 111-step fall to 1.
